title: 2025 DORA report: Insights to impact with Google and Thoughtworks
summary: DORA's Nathan Harvey and ThoughtWorks on the 2025 DORA report: AI as amplifier, throughput up but instability up, AI capabilities model.

assertions.quote: AI's primary role in software development is that of an amplifier

verdicts.note: DORA 2025 found AI amplifies existing engineering practices; strong fundamentals predict AI benefit.

assertions.quote: 90% of the people in our survey have said yes they are using AI in their professional work

verdicts.note: Stack Overflow 2025: ~84% use or plan to use AI tools, about half of professionals daily; JetBrains and DORA report similar figures.
Cites the 2025 Stack Overflow survey: 84% of professional developers are using or planning to use AI coding tools; the 'or planning' wording overstates current use.

In the volunteer prescreen at the end of 2024 (N=449, 92% professionals), 73.6% had prior experience with AI assistants, which is not the same as current regular use, and the sample was self-selected.

All 69 participants reported having used AI tools for software tasks before. This is a convenience sample of mostly students in three European universities and four companies, so it is weak evidence about professionals at large.

assertions.quote: This year we see throughput improving and stability dropping off

verdicts.note: DORA 2025 reports AI adoption now positively associated with throughput while still associated with higher delivery instability (change failure and rework).

DORA's 2024 survey found higher AI adoption associated with lower delivery stability (about 7.2% per 25% more adoption), as the claim says, but also with slightly lower throughput (about 1.5%), not higher; the claim's throughput half may rest on a later year's data.

assertions.quote: AI has a tendency to create some localized pockets of productivity. But that productivity gets ... swallowed up to downstream chaos

verdicts.note: DORA 2024/25 and Faros 2025 found individual output up while organizational delivery metrics stayed flat or worsened; review and integration become the bottleneck.

Anthropic reports a 67% rise in merged PRs per engineer per day after adopting Claude Code across the engineering org, but PR counts are a weak proxy for delivery. (Narrow setting, so it limits the claim rather than refuting it.)

DORA 2024 found AI adoption improved process measures (code review speed, approval speed, code quality) and individual productivity, yet was associated with lower delivery throughput and stability, concluding that improving the development process does not automatically improve software delivery; survey associations, not causal estimates.

assertions.quote: if our bottleneck is something like the code review process, simply generating more code isn't actually helping

verdicts.note: Studies of developer time show coding is a minority of work; DORA and Faros 2025 found individual coding gains often don't translate into delivery throughput.

Authors explain why field gains (26%) are smaller than lab gains: coding is only part of a developer's job and some tasks are less assistable, so time saved on coding only partly becomes extra output (interpretation, not directly measured).
Google: code review and rollout still need humans and quickly become the bottleneck, though AI still cut end-to-end migration time by about 50% or more, so the gains were real even though capped.

DORA's 2024 survey (about 3,000 professionals) found that a 25% rise in AI adoption went with faster code review and approval and higher individual productivity, yet an estimated 1.5% lower delivery throughput and 7.2% lower stability, which it attributes to larger changes; this supports limited end-to-end gains from faster coding, but it is cross-sectional and does not measure delivery time by phase or show coding was never the bottleneck.

In a survey of 484 Microsoft developers, coding took about 11% of the reported workweek, behind communication and meetings (12%), with debugging 9% and code review 5%; coding being a small share of time fits the claim, but self-reported time shares at one company do not measure what limits delivery.

assertions.quote: Access to internal data, working in small batches, and that clear and communicated stance

verdicts.note: These come from DORA's 2025 AI capabilities model, a survey-based correlational analysis; plausible and consistent with older DORA findings on small batches, but not causal evidence.

assertions.quote: don't set unrealistic expectations ... I expect 10x productivity gains

verdicts.note: Reports of token-maxing and resentment support it, but some mandated rollouts (e.g. Shopify, Coinbase) report adoption gains; evidence is anecdotal either way.

assertions.quote: about 59% report that working with AI is having a positive influence on the underlying quality of code

verdicts.note: DORA 2025 found ~59% reporting positive quality impact; it's self-report, which other studies show overstates measured effects.
Quality outcomes in the corpus are mixed and framed as trade-offs; the cited Fawzy et al. grey review found 68% of practitioners perceive vibe-coded output as 'fast but flawed'.

Developers reporting more workplace AI use rated their code's reusability and testability higher (+0.3 on the scale), but rated reliability and complexity no differently. The follow-up found lower maintainability.

In DORA's 2024 survey, 67% of respondents reported that AI is helping them improve their code; a self-report from a large survey, which the report says fits its estimated association of AI adoption with higher code quality.
